lead: CompTIA's server admin cert. It proves you can rack, set up, secure, back up and fix servers on Windows, Linux and virtual hosts, on premises or in a hybrid cloud. It's the natural step after A+ for anyone who runs a server room, a data closet or a cutter's servers.

v5.label: V5
v5.note: The only version you can take now. CompTIA hasn't announced a retirement date. A V6 (SK0-006) is in beta from Nov 12, 2026 to Feb 4, 2027, and CompTIA says the new exam launches in Summer 2027. Study V5 for any test date before then. CompTIA recommends A+ level knowledge and about two years of hands-on server work.
v5.onote: Official objective titles from CompTIA's SK0-005 objectives PDF. The line under each is a plain-language summary of its bullet list, not the full list.

domains.name: Server Hardware Installation and Management
obj: Given a scenario, install physical hardware
Racking and rail kits, enclosure sizes (1U, 2U, blades), cabling and cable management, power (PDUs, redundant power supplies, voltage) and cooling. Out-of-band management like iDRAC, iLO and IPMI.
Given a scenario, deploy and manage storage
RAID levels and controllers, drive types (HDD, SSD, NVMe), interfaces (SAS, SATA), shared storage (NAS, SAN with iSCSI and Fibre Channel) and capacity planning.
Given a scenario, perform server hardware maintenance
Firmware and BIOS/UEFI updates, hot-swap parts, replacing drives, fans and power supplies, and the lights and logs that tell you a part is failing.

domains.name: Server Administration
obj: Given a scenario, install server operating systems
Minimum requirements, install methods (media, network/PXE, image, unattended), partitions (GPT vs MBR) and filesystems (NTFS, ReFS, ext4, XFS, ZFS, VMFS).
Given a scenario, configure servers to use network infrastructure services
Static IP configuration, VLANs, default gateways, DNS and FQDNs, DHCP, NIC teaming and MAC addresses.
Given a scenario, configure and maintain server functions and features
Server roles (file, print, web, database, application, messaging, directory), baselines and performance metrics, data migration, and patching.
Explain the key concepts of high availability for servers
Clustering (active-active, active-passive, failover, failback, heartbeat), fault tolerance, load balancing and redundant network paths.
Summarize the purpose and operation of virtualization
Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisors, host vs guest, virtual networking, resource allocation and overprovisioning, and cloud models (public, private, hybrid).
Summarize scripting basics for server administration
Script types (bash, batch, PowerShell, VBScript), variables, loops, conditionals and comparisons, and common jobs like starting services, mapping drives and installing updates.
Explain the importance of asset management and documentation
Asset tags and inventory, the asset life cycle, warranty and support contracts, diagrams, baselines, runbooks and change logs.
Explain licensing concepts
Per-instance, per-user, per-core, per-socket and site licenses, subscriptions, open source, and license counts in virtual machines.

domains.name: Security and Disaster Recovery
obj: Summarize data security concepts
Encryption at rest and in transit, data retention, data storage, and UEFI/BIOS and boot passwords.
Summarize physical security concepts
Locks, bezels, badges, mantraps, cameras, guards and the layers of a secure server room.
Explain important concepts pertaining to identity and access management for server administration
User, group and service accounts, least privilege, role-based access, MFA, single sign-on and auditing who did what.
Explain data security risks and mitigation strategies
Insider threats, data loss, unwanted exposure and legal or regulatory concerns, and the controls that reduce them.
Given a scenario, apply server hardening methods
OS and firmware updates, disabling unused services, ports and accounts, host firewalls, antivirus and EDR, and secure baselines.
Summarize proper server decommissioning concepts
Wiping or destroying media, removing the server from DNS, monitoring and inventory, recycling, and documenting each step.
Explain the importance of backups and restores
Full, incremental, differential and snapshot backups, media and rotation, on-site vs off-site copies, and testing restores.
Explain the importance of disaster recovery
Hot, warm and cold sites, cloud DR, replication, RTO and RPO, and testing the plan with tabletops and failovers.

domains.name: Troubleshooting
obj: Explain the troubleshooting theory and methodology
CompTIA's steps: identify the problem, form a theory, test it, plan and fix, verify, and document.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot common hardware failures
POST errors, beep codes, failing memory and drives, overheating, power supply faults and misbehaving firmware.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot storage problems
Degraded or failed arrays, controller and cache failures, full disks, slow I/O, mount and boot problems, and data loss.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot common OS and software problems
Boot failures, logon problems, services that won't start, memory leaks, bad patches and drivers, and crashes.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot network connectivity issues
No IP, APIPA addresses, wrong gateway or mask, DNS failures, VLAN mistakes, bad cables and IP conflicts.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot security problems
Permission and access issues, failed logins, open ports, malware, rogue processes and services, and certificate problems.

It adds edge and hyperconverged infrastructure, infrastructure as code, containers, AI in server management, zero trust and SBOMs. Use this tab to see what's coming; study V5 to test now.

domains.name: Planning and Deployment
obj: Given a scenario, deploy physical hardware
Hardware compatibility lists, CPU, RAM and GPU choices, form factors, storage and redundancy, cabling, out-of-band management, UEFI vs BIOS, power and rack placement.
Compare and contrast concepts related to scaling infrastructure
Hyperconverged and edge computing, software-defined infrastructure and infrastructure as code, hypervisors and containers, and cloud models.
Given a scenario, install server operating systems
Requirements, Secure Boot, install media and methods, network deployment, filesystems, partitions, LVM and block size.

domains.name: Configuration and Administration
obj: Given a scenario, analyze requirements to configure servers
Filesystems, partitions and volumes, block size, network services (IP, VLANs, DNS, DHCP, firewall ports) and CPU and memory settings.
Given a scenario, configure and maintain common services
Server roles, hybrid cloud links, admin interfaces and command-line tools.
Given a scenario, apply virtualization to workloads
P2V and V2V migration, virtual networks, containers, rightsizing, hypervisor settings and device passthrough.
Given a scenario, implement high availability
Clustering, load balancing, NIC teaming, failover, RAID, hot-swap parts and scaling up vs out.
Given a scenario, use scripting, automation and orchestration
Shell, batch, Python and other scripts, scheduling, orchestration tools, script best practices and version control.
Explain the use of AI in server management
Diagnosis, research, automation, forecasting and data analysis, plus ethics and the permissions AI tools get.

domains.name: Security and Compliance
obj: Summarize common data security concepts
The data life cycle, encryption (including post-quantum), certificates and CAs, control types, and scans and pentests.
Explain policies, procedures and compliance
DR sites and tests, PII handling, frameworks, runbooks, RTO, RPO and SLAs, BIA, change management, audits, baselines and risk.
Given a scenario, implement backup, retention and recovery
Immutable and air-gapped backups, the 3-2-1 rule, backup types and validation, replication and deduplication.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot basic identity and access issues
Zero trust, authentication and network security problems: permissions, device trust, OTP, time sync, VLANs and expired certificates.
Given a scenario, implement server hardening
Turning off what isn't needed, credential and BIOS hardening, drive encryption, physical, logical and network controls, and DLP.
Apply patch management best practices
Scheduling, testing, rollback, trusted sources, validation, SBOMs, documentation and patch types.

domains.name: Data Center Operations
obj: Explain environmental considerations
HVAC, hot and cold aisles, blanking panels, fire suppression, environmental monitoring and liquid cooling.
Explain safety and health considerations
Personal and equipment safety, ergonomics, PPE, emergency plans and disposing of batteries and chemicals.
Explain power considerations
Power limits, UPS types, voltage, PDUs, plug types, outages, generators and redundant feeds.
Given a scenario, apply connectivity solutions
Storage and network connectors, fiber and transceivers, Ethernet, failover links, demarc, out-of-band access and cable management.
Explain security and access solutions
Logical controls like IAM and geofencing, and physical ones like badges, biometrics, fences and visitor logs.

domains.name: Performance Management and Troubleshooting
obj: Given a scenario, use observability strategies
Logs, alerts, baselines, load and utilization metrics, trends and dashboards.
Given a scenario, use tools to identify server issues
Crash carts and KVMs, plus network, process, file and storage tools.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot common hardware issues
Predictive failures, memory errors, crashes, batteries, POST codes, overheating and power supplies.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot common OS and software issues
Memory leaks, corruption, boot and logon failures, hung apps, slow systems, drivers and failed patches.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot common storage issues
Degraded RAID, drive and cache failures, full disks, slow I/O, mounts, failed restores and unexpected encryption.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot common network connectivity issues
Domain join failures, service access, bad cables, name resolution, DHCP and IP conflicts.
Given a scenario, troubleshoot common security issues
Login and permission problems, open ports, rogue processes, unauthorized access, file integrity and privilege escalation.

extras.title: RAID at a glance
rows: Fast, but no protection. One drive fails and everything is gone. Min 2 drives.
Two copies. Survives one drive failure; you get half the raw space. Min 2 drives.
Survives one failure; you lose one drive of space. Slow rebuilds on big drives. Min 3.
Survives two failures at once; you lose two drives of space. Min 4.
Fast and survives one failure per mirror; half the raw space. Min 4.
Sits idle and starts rebuilding the array as soon as a drive fails.

extras.title: Backup types
rows: Slowest to run, fastest to restore: you need just one set.
Fastest to run. A restore needs the full plus every incremental since.
Grows each day. A restore needs the full plus the latest differential.
Quick rollback, but it usually lives on the same storage. Not a real backup alone.
3 copies, on 2 kinds of media, with 1 off site. Keep 1 offline or immutable too.

extras.title: Disaster recovery terms
rows: How much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RPO 4 h means back up at least every 4 hours.
How long the service can be down before it hurts the mission.
Running gear and current data. Fail over in minutes. The most expensive.
Gear in place, data a bit behind. Hours to a day to bring up.
An empty room with power and cooling. Days or weeks to get running. The cheapest.
The team walks through the plan on paper. Finds gaps without touching production.

extras.title: CompTIA's troubleshooting method
rows: Identify the problem: ask users, check logs, find what changed, and back up before you touch anything.
Establish a theory of probable cause. Question the obvious.
Test the theory. If it's wrong, form a new one or escalate.
Make a plan of action, think about its side effects, and get change approval.
Carry out the fix, or escalate it.
Verify the whole system works and take steps so it doesn't happen again.
Document what you found, what you did and how it turned out.

method: Use the four V5 domains as your checklist. Administration and Troubleshooting are over half the exam.
Set up a small lab on your own PC: a free hypervisor, one Windows Server evaluation VM and one Linux VM. Give them static IPs, DNS and a file share.
Pull a virtual disk out of a RAID set, fill a volume, stop a service, give a VM the wrong gateway. Then fix each one with the 4.0 steps.
Flashcards for RAID levels, backup types, RPO vs RTO, DR site types, filesystems and license models.
Timed practice exams with PBQs. Review every miss and aim for 85%+ twice in a row before you book.
tips: Many questions ask what to do FIRST or NEXT. Walk CompTIA's seven troubleshooting steps in order, and back up before you change anything.
Usable space for each RAID level and the minimum number of drives come up often. Work a few examples by hand.
LEAST expensive, FASTEST restore, MOST secure: one word decides between two good answers.
They often come first and eat time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.

quiz.q: A file server needs the most usable space from six 4 TB drives, and it must keep running if any TWO drives fail at the same time. Which RAID level fits?
o: RAID 6 (16 TB usable)
Right. Double parity costs two drives of space (6 − 2 = 4 drives × 4 TB) and survives any two failures.
RAID 5 (20 TB usable)
More space, but single parity survives only one failure. A second failure during a rebuild loses the array.
RAID 10 (12 TB usable)
RAID 10 can survive two failures only if they hit different mirrors. Two drives in the same mirror kill it, and it gives less space.
RAID 0 (24 TB usable)
All the space, but no protection at all. Any single failure loses everything.

quiz.q: A remote site's server has hung and won't answer RDP or SSH. Nobody is on site. What lets you power-cycle it and watch it boot from your desk?
o: Its out-of-band management card (iDRAC, iLO or IPMI)
Right. The management controller has its own network port and power, so it works even when the OS is dead.
Wake-on-LAN
Wake-on-LAN can turn a powered-off machine on, but it can't reset a hung one or show you the console.
A KVM switch in the rack
A KVM only helps someone standing in the server room. Nobody is on site.
Remote PowerShell
PowerShell remoting runs on the OS, which is hung. It won't answer either.

quiz.q: A new DHCP and DNS server reboots and comes up as 169.254.12.7. Clients can't find it. What should the admin do?
o: Give it a static IP address
Right. Infrastructure servers need an address that never changes. 169.254.x.x (APIPA) means it asked for DHCP and nobody answered.
Renew its DHCP lease
It IS the DHCP server, and servers that others depend on shouldn't rely on leases at all.
Add a DNS suffix
A suffix doesn't help when the server has no valid address.
Turn on NIC teaming
Teaming adds redundancy and bandwidth. It doesn't give the server an address.

quiz.q: Two database nodes run as a cluster. Only one serves users; the other takes over if the first fails. They watch each other over a private link. What is this setup?
o: An active-passive cluster with a heartbeat
Right. One node works, one waits. The heartbeat on the private link tells the standby when to take over.
An active-active cluster with load balancing
In active-active, both nodes serve users at the same time.
RAID 1 across two servers
RAID mirrors drives inside one system. This is two whole servers.
A snapshot schedule
Snapshots are point-in-time copies. They don't take over when a server dies.

quiz.q: A VMware host runs 20 VMs with 4 vCPUs each on 32 physical cores. Users say everything is slow, and the CPU ready time is very high. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: CPU overprovisioning: 80 vCPUs are fighting for 32 cores
Right. High ready time means VMs are waiting for a free physical core. Rightsize the VMs or add hosts.
The VMs use thin-provisioned disks
Thin disks affect storage space, not CPU wait time.
The host runs a Type 1 hypervisor
Type 1 is the normal, faster choice for servers.
The VMs need more RAM
Memory pressure shows up as ballooning and swapping, not CPU ready time.

quiz.q: A database vendor licenses per core. You move the database from an old 2 x 8-core server to a new 2 x 16-core server. What happens to licensing?
o: You likely need twice as many core licenses
Right. Per-core licensing counts physical cores (32 now vs 16 before), even if the database doesn't need them all.
Nothing, it's still one server
That's per-instance or per-server licensing. This vendor counts cores.
You need licenses per user instead
The license model doesn't change because the hardware did.
Fewer licenses, because the new CPUs are faster
Per-core counts cores, not speed.

quiz.q: A mission system can lose at most 15 minutes of data and must be back within 2 hours. Which pair of targets does this describe?
o: RPO 15 minutes, RTO 2 hours
Right. RPO is how much data you can lose; RTO is how long you can be down.
RTO 15 minutes, RPO 2 hours
Swapped. Data loss is RPO, downtime is RTO.
MTBF 15 minutes, MTTR 2 hours
MTBF and MTTR measure hardware reliability and repair time, not recovery targets.
SLA 15 minutes, BIA 2 hours
An SLA is an agreement and a BIA is an analysis. Neither is a recovery target.

quiz.q: Backups run as a full on Sunday and an incremental each other night. The server dies Thursday morning. What do you need to restore?
o: Sunday's full plus Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday's incrementals
Right. Each incremental only holds changes since the night before, so you need the full and every incremental after it, in order.
Sunday's full plus Wednesday's incremental
That would work with differentials. Incrementals each hold one day.
Only Wednesday's incremental
An incremental is just one day's changes. It can't rebuild the server alone.
Only Sunday's full
You'd lose everything from Monday to Wednesday.

quiz.q: A server holding personnel records is being retired, and its drives will be recycled by a contractor. What should happen to the drives FIRST?
o: Sanitize or destroy them per policy and document it
Right. Data must be wiped to the required standard (or the drives shredded) and recorded before any drive leaves your control.
Delete the files and format the drives
Deleted and formatted data can usually be recovered.
Remove the server from Active Directory
Do that too, but the data on the drives is the risk that walks out the door.
Pull the drives and store them in a desk
Unwiped drives in a desk are still a data spill waiting to happen.

quiz.q: A new web server has passed testing. Which hardening step is MOST important before it goes into production?
o: Disable the services, ports and accounts it doesn't need
Right. Every service and account you remove is one less way in. That's the core of hardening.
Move the web service to a non-standard port
Hiding a port cuts noise but isn't real protection, and it can break clients.
Give the service account local admin to avoid errors
That's the opposite of least privilege. A compromise would get admin rights.
Turn off logging to save disk space
Logs are how you notice and investigate attacks. Keep them.

quiz.q: A RAID 5 array shows Degraded after a drive failure. You've replaced the drive and the rebuild has started. What should you do NEXT?
o: Watch the rebuild and confirm the latest backup is good
Right. A second failure during a rebuild loses a RAID 5 array, so know your backup works and avoid heavy load until it finishes.
Reboot the server to speed up the rebuild
A reboot can interrupt the rebuild and add risk.
Pull the other drives to check them
Removing another drive from a degraded RAID 5 destroys the array.
Convert the array to RAID 0
RAID 0 has no protection, and converting mid-rebuild is reckless.

quiz.q: Users can reach a file server by IP (\\10.1.4.20) but not by name (\\fs01). Other servers resolve fine. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: fs01 has a missing or wrong DNS record
Right. The network path works (IP works), so only name resolution for this one server is broken. Check its A record.
The server's default gateway is wrong
Then users on other subnets couldn't reach it by IP either.
The SMB service is stopped
Then access by IP would fail too.
A bad network cable
A bad cable breaks access by IP as well as by name.

quiz.q: A server slows down a little more every day and is fine right after a reboot. Task Manager shows one service's memory use climbing steadily. What is this?
o: A memory leak in that service
Right. Memory that grows and never comes back until a restart is the classic leak. Patch the service or schedule restarts until it's fixed.
A failing hard drive
Drive trouble shows up as I/O errors and slow disk, not steadily climbing memory.
CPU overheating
Heat causes throttling and crashes, not one process's memory growing.
A DNS failure
DNS problems break name lookups. They don't eat memory.

quiz.q: You want every new server built the same way, from a file kept in Git, so builds are repeatable and changes are reviewed. Which practice is this?
o: Infrastructure as code
Right. The build is described in code, kept in version control and applied by a tool, so every build matches.
A golden image copied by hand
An image helps, but hand copies drift, and nobody reviews changes to a file in Git.
Overprovisioning
Overprovisioning is giving out more virtual resources than physically exist. It's unrelated.
P2V migration
P2V turns a physical server into a VM. It doesn't build new ones.

quiz.q: Ransomware encrypted the file servers AND the backup server they write to. Which backup feature would have saved the data?
o: Immutable or air-gapped backup copies
Right. An immutable or offline copy can't be changed or deleted by an attacker who owns the network.
Daily differential backups
Differentials on the same reachable backup server get encrypted too.
Deduplication
Dedup saves space. It doesn't protect copies from being encrypted.
More frequent snapshots on the same storage
Snapshots on the same storage are reachable and often deleted first by ransomware.

quiz.q: Before patching, your team checks a software bill of materials (SBOM) for a vendor app. What does the SBOM tell you?
o: Which components and libraries are inside the software
Right. With the SBOM you can see if the app includes a library that has a new vulnerability, like a vulnerable logging library.
The vendor's patch release schedule
That's in the vendor's support policy, not the SBOM.
Which servers the app is installed on
That's your asset inventory.
The app's license cost
An SBOM lists parts, not prices.

quiz.q: Servers in the back of a rack overheat even though the room is cold. The rack has empty spaces between servers. What is the BEST first fix?
o: Install blanking panels in the empty spaces
Right. Gaps let hot exhaust loop back to the front intakes. Blanking panels keep the hot and cold aisles apart.
Turn the room temperature down further
Colder air doesn't help if hot exhaust keeps mixing in at the intakes.
Add a second UPS
A UPS is about power, not airflow.
Mount the servers backward
That blows hot air into the cold aisle and makes it worse.

pbqs.title: Pick the RAID for each server
pbqs.scenario: Your shop is building five new servers. For each one, pick the RAID level that BEST fits the need and the fewest drives it needs. Some options aren't used.

rows.req: Boot drives for a domain controller: simple, survives one failure
rows.why: A two-drive mirror is the classic boot volume: one drive can fail and the server keeps running.

rows.req: Scratch space for video renders, rebuilt nightly; speed is all that matters
rows.why: Striping is fastest and the data is disposable, so no protection is needed.

rows.req: Busy database: fast writes and survives a drive failure
rows.why: RAID 10 has no parity math on writes and survives one failure per mirror. It needs at least four drives.

rows.req: Large archive share: most space, must survive two failures at once
rows.why: Double parity survives any two failures. RAID 6 needs at least four drives.

rows.req: Small file server on a tight budget: survives one failure, keeps the most space
rows.why: Single parity loses just one drive of space. RAID 5 needs at least three drives.

pbqs.title: Diagnose six server tickets
pbqs.scenario: Six tickets came in overnight. Read each clue and pick the most likely cause. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
> ipconfig
IPv4 Address. . . . . . . : 169.254.88.14
Subnet Mask . . . . . . . : 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway . . . . . :
items.why: A 169.254 (APIPA) address means the server asked for an address and no DHCP server answered. Check the scope, or give the server a static IP.

items.log:
03:12 Physical disk 0:1:3 state changed: Online -> Failed
03:12 Virtual disk 1 (RAID 5) state changed: Optimal -> Degraded
items.why: One drive failed and the array is running without protection. Replace the drive and let it rebuild.

items.log:
Your connection isn't private
NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID
issued to: intranet.unit.example
valid until: 2026-11-13
items.why: The certificate's valid-until date has passed. Renew it and bind the new one to the site.

items.log:
Job 'Nightly-Files' failed: logon failure
Event 4740: A user account was locked out.
Account: svc-backup
items.why: The service account was locked, likely from an old password stored somewhere. Unlock it and fix the stored credential.

items.log:
Mon spoolsv.exe 410 MB
Wed spoolsv.exe 1.9 GB
Fri spoolsv.exe 3.6 GB
After reboot: spoolsv.exe 380 MB
items.why: Memory grows every day and only drops after a reboot: a classic leak. Patch the driver or service.

items.log:
System event: CPU1 temperature 97 C (critical)
System event: Processor throttling enabled
Fan 3: 0 RPM
items.why: A dead fan let the CPU overheat and throttle. Replace the fan and check airflow.
